]]>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 19:31:49 +0000https://rdfandsparql.com/rdf12-sparq12-cheat-sheetMKolchinhttps://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50249649https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50249649<![CDATA[Show HN: Flowfile – Open-source visual ETL that round-trips to Python (Polars)]]>Hi HN, I'm Edward, the author of Flowfile.

Flowfile is a visual ETL tool built on Polars. You build pipelines on a canvas, and every flow is also Python code. You can export it or write code with the FlowFrame API (Polars-like) and it shows up as a visual graph (or vice versa - keep reading).

Flowfile is what it is today because I believe we are spending too much time translating non-technical and technical implementations of data problems. Sometimes visual works better, and sometimes code. You should be able to choose whichever is easiest, without fully committing to one way of working. Flowfile solves this by standardizing the backend component without favoring either visual or code.

Which brings me to Flowfile's newest feature: notebook mode. The flow opens as Python cells that stay in sync with the canvas. If you add a filter (df.filter(...)) in a cell, it appears on the canvas. And it also works the other way around: if you add a sort on the canvas, it appears as a .sort(...) in the notebook. So now you can switch between visual and code without making a total mess of it under the hood.

It also has a data catalog, a scheduler, sandboxed Python execution, etc.. It's MIT licensed, and `pip install flowfile` installs all dependencies.

Github: https://github.com/edwardvaneechoud/Flowfile

I'd love feedback, especially on the notebook mode.

Since its first release more than half a year ago, I've added multiplayer support, so you can now host a game and play with friends (or colleagues during a meeting?); Up to 8 players. I've also substantially improved the visuals, lighting, physics, and overall gameplay. A friend and I ended up spending the entire weekend playing through the game from start to finish.

The progression takes you from gathering wood and building a shelter to crafting equipment, exploring caves, finding diamonds, crossing the Nether, and fighting the Ender Dragon. There are villages, farming, collaborative building, PvP, and player chat along the way.

It's open source under the AGPL-3.0 license, with downloadable builds for Linux, macOS, and Windows.

Gameplay demo video: https://youtu.be/nn37_15dLFM Installation and controls: https://pagel-s.github.io/termcraft/

It's not perfect, but I'd love to hear your feedback and experiences with the game. Contributions are also more than welcome!

]]>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 17:32:24 +0000https://covenant-common.github.io/covenant-docs/jupiehttps://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50247633https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50247633<![CDATA[Show HN: RPI Pico (RP2040) PIO Emulator Package for Go]]>I have been developing a bus communication protocol for a while using the Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040)'s programmable IO (PIO) hardware (basically- 8 tiny processors that run assembly programs to manipulate GPIO pins) and I needed some way of testing my programs, as the real hardware is undebuggable.

Unfortunately, none of the existing emulators I could find supported connecting multiple RP2040s together, and they each had a few different missing bits of functionality, so I decided to make my own!

My emulator supports running multiple RP2040s electrically connected together, and emulates the whole of their PIO blocks (all 8 processors each), along with all of the more niche inter-processor interactions and GPIO functionality I could possibly find in the datasheet.

I built it as a Go package so that it can be used inside of other programs; I intend on using it myself inside a test suite against my in-development protocol.

I've spent quite a long time checking and double-checking most of the logic so it is as complete and accurate as I can make it, but if you spot anything amiss, I'd really appreciate the feedback.

Thanks for checking it out! Hope it can be useful to other RP2040 users.

]]>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 17:06:14 +0000https://github.com/ekzhang/resinekzhanghttps://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50247183https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50247183<![CDATA[Show HN: pw-repl - A Playwright-powered REPL for you and your agents to share]]>For the busy people out there, the GitHub repo has a demo video so you can see if this is worth your time: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

The video was created by Opus 5.5; I just asked it to create a demo video (it has a 'record' tool), so I think this is a good idea of how well it can work with the tool.

---

pw-repl is a tool that makes it easy for you and your agents to work with Playwright+CDP in a browser (your current headed session, or a headless one, or both at the same time; take your pick).

It's basically a Playwright-powered swiss army knife that helps you and agents poke around your browser: Try out different features of a website, break things (e.g. mock backend responses), take screenshots, record videos, etc.

The GitHub repo shows a video, recorded by an agent using pw-repl: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

One cool thing it can do: create videos of bug reports. You can tell an agent about a bug and to use pw-repl to capture it, and it can record a video with the built-in toast feature to narrate its actions, and show a virtual mouse to simulate actions on the screen, as if it were a user. It's also useful for capturing screenshots (which can be combined with the toast and highlight tools to emphasize certain elements or information), and has many useful features that can help agents to use it efficiently.

This isn't intended to be commercialized in any way. It's just a neat tool that I (with Claude's help) cobbled together. It's completely vibe-coded, and is intended mainly as a debugging aid. I use all the time, and hope it may be helpful for others.

It's basically just Playwright + CDP under the hood, but has some extra tools and an interface that make it easier for agents to work with.

The quickest way to try it out is to tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background --launch`, which starts a headless Chromium of its own. No browser setup needed. (If you don't like such `curl | bash`-esque installation instructions, read the code, or get your agent to take a look at it.)

To use it in your own browser instead, start Chrome with CDP enabled (`chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir="$HOME/.config/chrome-debug"`), and tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background`. (The separate `--user-data-dir` is needed because recent versions of Chrome don't open the debugging port on your default profile.)

It also can generate a skill so that you can just run `/pw-repl do some stuff`. Get your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest skill > /pw-repl/SKILL.md` (e.g. `~/.claude/skills/pw-repl/SKILL.md` for Claude Code).

NOTE: This has only been tested on my Linux machine, so not sure if it will work on macOS. It should, but I haven't tried it out personally.

Fun fact: This tool was originally a random REPL that Claude generated on-the-fly to do some random thing. I saw it and was blown away, so I got Claude to make it into its own application. I suspect that Claude may have taken "inspiration" from an existing project with a similar name, so credit where credit is due to this other `playwright-repl` package: https://github.com/stevez/playwright-repl
